records.responseText:
For a small insurance agency, I’d narrow it to these three:

Pick	Best for	Approx. cost	Why
Sonant AI	Best overall for P&C agencies	Custom	Insurance-specific; connects directly to EZLynx, Applied Epic, HawkSoft, AMS360, AgencyZoom, etc.
Rosie AI – Scale	Best value for a small agency	$149/mo	1,000 minutes, English/Spanish, appointment booking, warm/live transfers, Zapier
Smith.ai	Best when human backup matters	From $150/mo for 75 AI calls	AI answers first; live human agents can take over complicated calls
My recommendation

If you use an AMS like EZLynx, HawkSoft, AMS360, Applied Epic, AgencyZoom, QQCatalyst, or Momentum → demo Sonant first. It is built specifically for P&C insurance and can identify callers, handle quote/service intake, route calls, and write notes/tasks back into the AMS. It also supports warm transfers and is SOC 2 Type II compliant. 
Sonant
+1

That AMS integration is a big deal. A generic AI receptionist may take a beautiful message, but your CSR still has to open the customer record and enter everything manually. Sonant can eliminate much of that duplicate work. 
Sonant
+1

The drawback is Sonant doesn't publish simple small-business pricing, so it may be more system than a 1–5 person agency needs. 
Sonant

Best bang for the buck: Rosie

If you mainly want someone to answer every call, determine why they're calling, capture new-business leads, schedule appointments and transfer important calls, I'd probably choose Rosie Scale at $149/month.

It currently includes 1,000 minutes/month, direct calendar booking, warm transfers, live transfers, texts during calls, English and Spanish, call summaries/transcripts/recordings, and Zapier integration. 
Hey Rosie

That's an unusually strong package for a small agency.

When I'd choose Smith.ai

Smith.ai is particularly attractive if you're nervous about an AI getting stuck with an upset insured, complicated claim situation, or unusual question. Its AI can escalate to live North America-based receptionists, while still providing 24/7 answering, lead qualification, scheduling, bilingual handling, warm transfers, recordings and integrations. 
Smith.ai
+1

The downside is cost at higher call volume. The current Pro AI plan starts around $150/month for 75 calls, with additional calls charged separately. 
Smith.ai

One important insurance rule

Whichever you choose, I would configure the AI to never interpret coverage, recommend limits, promise that something is covered, bind coverage, or make policy changes requiring licensed judgment. Use it for intake and service routing:

“New quote → collect information → producer.”
“Claim → collect basic details → carrier/CSR.”
“Billing → appropriate carrier/CSR.”
“Policy change → collect request → licensed staff.”
“Certificate/COI → collect request → service team/approved automated workflow.”

That setup gets most of the labor savings without creating unnecessary E&O exposure.

My ranking for a typical small independent agency: Sonant if you want deep AMS automation; Rosie if you want the best value and fast deployment; Smith.ai if human backup is your highest priority.

If you tell me (1) how many employees you have, (2) approximately how many calls you get per day, and (3) whether you use EZLynx, HawkSoft, Applied Epic, AMS360, AgencyZoom, etc., I can narrow it down to the one I'd buy for your agency and estimate the monthly cost.

records.responseText:
Small insurance agencies usually handle after-hours missed calls with some combination of voicemail, call forwarding, and next-business-day follow-up.

The most common setups are:

Voicemail + callback queue: The caller leaves a message, and staff return it the next morning. This is cheapest, but leads can go cold quickly.

Forwarding to the owner or producer: Calls ring a personal cell after hours. This can work for very small agencies, but it gets intrusive fast.

Answering service: A live receptionist takes the caller’s name, number, reason for calling, and urgency, then sends the agency a message or escalates emergencies.

Automated text-back: If a call is missed, the system immediately texts something like, “Sorry we missed you—are you calling about a quote, policy change, claim, or something else?” This is increasingly useful for capturing leads without staffing phones all night.

AI/virtual receptionist: Some agencies use a phone agent that can answer basic questions, collect quote information, schedule callbacks, and route urgent matters.

Carrier claims routing: For an actual accident, loss, or roadside issue, the after-hours message often directs the customer to the insurance carrier’s 24/7 claims line rather than trying to handle the claim at the agency.

A good small-agency workflow is usually: answer immediately if possible → capture the caller’s intent → distinguish new lead vs. existing customer vs. claim → send urgent claims to the carrier → create a callback task for everything else.

The biggest business issue is usually new quote calls. Someone shopping for auto, home, or commercial insurance may call several agencies in a row, so a missed call that sits in voicemail until the next morning can easily become a lost sale.

If you're looking at this from a business/automation angle, I can also break down exactly what a 5–20 person insurance agency typically needs in an after-hours call system, including what they would realistically pay for it.

records.responseText:
The biggest difference is that an insurance-specific AI receptionist is designed to complete insurance workflows, while a general answering service is primarily designed to make sure somebody answers the phone.

Area	Insurance-specific AI receptionist	General answering service
Insurance vocabulary	Understands FNOL, COIs, renewals, endorsements, policy numbers, lines of business, etc.	Usually follows a script; insurance knowledge varies
Quote intake	Can ask different questions for auto, home, commercial, life, etc., and structure the lead	Typically captures name, number, reason for calling; sophisticated services can do scripted qualification
Claims	Can collect structured FNOL details and route emergencies according to agency rules	Usually takes a message or transfers the caller
AMS/CRM integration	Strong products can identify clients, retrieve permitted information, and write notes into systems such as Applied Epic, EZLynx, AMS360, HawkSoft, or NowCerts	More commonly sends messages into a portal/email/CRM, although some general services offer CRM integrations
COI/service requests	May initiate COI, policy-change, billing, or callback workflows	Usually records the request for agency staff
Availability	24/7 and can typically handle many simultaneous calls	Human services can also be 24/7, but capacity depends on staffing
Consistency	Same rules/questions every call	Quality can vary somewhat between operators
Empathy / unusual situations	Improving, but complex or emotional conversations should have good human escalation	Live humans generally handle ambiguity, upset callers, and unusual situations better
Cost model	Usually subscription, usage-based AI, or a combination; high call volumes can be economical	Live services commonly charge by receptionist minute or call
Setup	More involved because workflows, AMS permissions, escalation rules, knowledge base and guardrails matter	Usually easier: greeting + script + routing instructions

Insurance-native systems currently advertise features such as structured FNOL intake, insurance-specific quote qualification, appointment scheduling, AMS write-back, caller verification, and escalation to licensed staff rather than attempting to resolve everything themselves. 
Sonant
+3
PhoneAgent.ai
+3
navaia
+3

Where insurance AI has the clearest advantage

For an agency getting a lot of repetitive calls, the difference can be substantial. Instead of receiving:

“John Smith called about his auto policy. Please call him back.”

your team can receive something closer to:

Existing customer → auto policy → wants to add a vehicle → VIN/model captured → effective date requested → identity verified → request logged in AMS → CSR notified.

That structured workflow is the main value proposition—not simply having an AI-sounding person answer the phone.

It's particularly useful for new-business qualification, after-hours calls, renewal scheduling, basic service requests, FNOL collection, COI intake and catastrophe-driven call spikes. Several insurance-focused platforms explicitly design around those workflows. 
InsuraMate AI
+2
InsuraMate AI
+2

Where a general live answering service can be better

Human answering services still have an advantage when conversations are unpredictable or emotionally sensitive. A good operator can recognize that an angry insured, confused elderly customer, distressed claimant, or high-value commercial client needs something outside the normal script.

And today's general services aren't necessarily primitive. For example, Ruby offers 24/7 live receptionists, scheduling, intake and bilingual answering, while AnswerConnect offers 24/7 human answering, customizable scripts and CRM integrations. 
Ruby - 24/7 Virtual Receptionists
+1

The tradeoff is economics. As of September 2026, Ruby publishes plans such as $250/month for 50 receptionist minutes, while AnswerConnect publishes $350/month for 200 minutes, with overage charges on its entry plan. That means human answering costs can increase considerably as call duration and volume rise. 
Ruby - 24/7 Virtual Receptionists
+1

One important caveat: don't confuse “insurance-trained” with “licensed”

An AI being able to recognize insurance terminology doesn't mean you should allow it to freely interpret coverage, recommend limits, make representations about whether a loss is covered, or perform activities requiring a license.

A well-designed deployment therefore looks more like:

AI handles → identify → authenticate → collect → classify → schedule → document → route

rather than:

AI handles → interpret policy → recommend coverage → promise claim outcome.

AI use in insurance is also receiving increasing regulatory attention. The NAIC's AI Model Bulletin emphasizes that actions or decisions supported by AI remain subject to applicable insurance laws and calls for appropriate governance and controls. 
NAIC
+1

What I'd choose for an insurance agency

For most agencies, I wouldn't frame the decision as AI versus humans. The strongest model is usually:

insurance AI receptionist for Tier-1 calls → licensed CSR/producer for anything consequential.

That gives you 24/7 answering and automated intake without asking AI to do the part of insurance where human judgment, licensing, or relationship management matters.

If you're evaluating vendors, the five questions I'd put at the top of the RFP are (1) which AMS actions are genuinely native rather than Zapier/email workarounds, (2) what happens when confidence is low, (3) exactly what policy information the AI may disclose, (4) how licensing/coverage questions are blocked and escalated, and (5) whether you can audit every call and AMS action. Those tell you considerably more than how realistic the demo voice sounds.
